evidence.label: Arithmetic classification and non-Pisot singularity for Bernoulli convolutions

headline: Claimed singular Bernoulli convolutions beyond Pisot reciprocals, plus an arithmetic test for every parameter.
scope: Unbiased Bernoulli convolutions, the random sums of ±λⁿ with fair signs, for every λ between 0 and 1.
plain: Add up ±1 ± λ ± λ² and so on, choosing each sign by a fair coin flip. The result has a density or sits on a set of zero length, and for many λ it was unknown which. Above one half, every known zero-length case had 1/λ equal to a Pisot number, following Erdős in 1939. This paper claims new zero-length cases, at one over each degree-four Salem number between 1 and 2, and at one more number. It also claims an exact arithmetic test for every λ, though not a finite procedure.
doesNot: This does not give a finite procedure that decides, for a given λ, which of the two cases holds.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Erdős, singularity when 1/λ is a Pisot number
scorecard.significanceWhy: Singular examples beyond Pisot reciprocals are recorded as open in the recent literature the paper cites.

explanation:
Flip a fair coin again and again. Heads adds a plus sign, tails a minus sign. Now add ±1 ± λ ± λ² ± λ³ and so on, where λ is a fixed number between 0 and 1. The sum is a random number. Its probability law is called the unbiased Bernoulli convolution for λ. Take λ = 1/2. Then the sum is spread perfectly evenly over the interval from −2 to 2.

Now take λ = 1/3. Fix the first ten signs, which allows 1,024 choices. The rest of the sum then stays inside a window of width 3 × (1/3)¹⁰. So all outcomes sit inside 1,024 short intervals. Their total length is 3 × (2/3)¹⁰, about 0.052. With more flips that total keeps shrinking towards zero. The law is singular: all its probability sits on a set of zero total length. This simple covering argument works for every λ below 1/2.

The hard range is λ between 1/2 and 1. Since 1935 it has been known that each such law has a pure type. It is either singular or absolutely continuous, meaning it has a density, like a smooth histogram. The classification problem asks which type holds for each λ.

Number theory enters here. A Pisot number is a number above 1 that solves a polynomial with whole-number coefficients and leading coefficient 1. Its other roots must all have size below 1. The golden ratio, about 1.618, is one. Its partner root is about −0.618. In 1939 Erdős proved the law is singular when 1/λ is a Pisot number. So λ ≈ 0.618 gives a singular law. In 1962 Garsia found a different class with a density. In 1995 Solomyak showed that almost every λ in the range has a density. In 2014 Shmerkin showed the possible exceptions form a very thin set, of dimension zero. Still, the recent literature lists one gap as open. No singular example was known whose 1/λ is not a Pisot number.

Salem numbers are the natural next suspects. A Salem number is like a Pisot number, but its other roots are 1/β and roots of size exactly 1. Take x⁴ − x³ − x² − x + 1. Its largest root is about 1.7221. Its other roots are about 0.5807, and a pair of complex roots of size exactly 1. In 1943 Salem showed that a key tool fails here. That tool, the Fourier transform, measures how strongly the law repeats at each frequency. For non-Pisot parameters it fades to zero, so it cannot prove singularity.

The paper claims to prove singularity at 1/β for every degree-four Salem number β between 1 and 2. That includes λ ≈ 1/1.7221 ≈ 0.5807 from the example. It claims the same for one root of an explicit degree-31 polynomial, between 1.8392 and 1.8393, which is not Pisot. For the Salem case, it builds certain wave-like averages from the Fourier transform. Under the Bernoulli convolution they stay concentrated, while under ordinary length they fade. That difference shows the law is singular.

The paper also claims a criterion for every λ. It uses finite lists of algebraic units, roots of polynomials with coefficients −1, 0 or 1. The law is singular exactly when such units approach λ from one side at a fixed geometric rate. This is an infinite approximation condition. It need not give a short test for a given number.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this result in the openai/math release. The degree-31 case comes with a Python script that checks its finite exact arithmetic. The paper supplies the analytic bounds linking that check to the infinite products in the proof. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proofs hold. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. A script checks only the finite arithmetic of the degree-31 case.

glossary.meaning: The probability law of ±1 ± λ ± λ² ± …, with each sign chosen by a fair coin.
Putting all probability on a set of zero total length, so no density exists.
Having a density, so probability is spread like a histogram with no zero-length pile-ups.
A root above 1 of a whole-coefficient polynomial with leading coefficient 1, whose other roots all have size below 1.
Like a Pisot number, but its other roots are 1/β and roots of size exactly 1.
A measure of how strongly a probability law repeats at each frequency.
A root of a whole-coefficient polynomial whose leading and constant coefficients are each 1 or −1.

claims.text: At λ = 1/2 the law is uniform on [−2, 2].
claims.sourceLine: at $\lambda=1/2$, $\nu_\lambda$ is uniform on $[-2,2]$.

claims.text: For λ below 1/2 an interval cover proves singularity.
claims.sourceLine: For $\lambda<1/2$, a direct interval cover proves singularity

claims.text: A singular measure gives full mass to a set of zero length.
claims.sourceLine: A measure is singular if it gives full mass to a Borel set of Lebesgue measure zero.

claims.text: Bernoulli convolutions are either singular or absolutely continuous.
claims.sourceLine: Bernoulli convolutions have pure type: they are either singular or absolutely continuous

claims.text: The interval from 1/2 to 1 holds the arithmetic difficulty.
claims.sourceLine: The interval $(1/2,1)$ presents the arithmetic difficulty.

claims.text: Definition of a Pisot number.
claims.sourceLine: is a real algebraic integer $\beta>1$ whose other conjugates have modulus less than one.

claims.text: Erdős proved singularity when 1/λ is Pisot.
claims.sourceLine: Erd\H{o}s proved singularity when $\lambda^{-1}$ is Pisot by showing that the Fourier transform does not tend to zero

claims.text: Garsia found absolute continuity for a different arithmetic class.
claims.sourceLine: Garsia subsequently established absolute continuity for a different arithmetic class

claims.text: Solomyak proved a density for almost every λ in the range.
claims.sourceLine: Solomyak proved that $\nu_\lambda$ has an $L^2$ density for Lebesgue-almost every $\lambda\in(1/2,1)$

claims.text: Shmerkin showed possible singular parameters form a set of dimension zero.
claims.sourceLine: Shmerkin proved that the possible singular parameters in this interval form a set of Hausdorff dimension zero

claims.text: Definition of a Salem number.
claims.sourceLine: is a real algebraic integer $\beta>1$ whose other conjugates consist of $\beta^{-1}$ and conjugates on the unit circle.

claims.text: Salem showed the Fourier transform tends to zero for non-Pisot parameters.
claims.sourceLine: Salem proved that the Fourier transform of $\nu_\lambda$ tends to zero whenever $\lambda^{-1}$ is not Pisot

claims.text: So Fourier nondecay cannot prove singularity for Salem parameters.
claims.sourceLine: Thus Fourier nondecay cannot prove singularity for Salem parameters.

claims.text: Non-Pisot singular examples are recorded as open.
claims.sourceLine: The existence of singular examples with non-Pisot reciprocal is explicitly recorded as open in the recent literature

claims.text: Every degree-four Salem number in (1,2) gives a singular law.
claims.sourceLine: Let $\beta\in(1,2)$ be a Salem number of degree four.

claims.sourceLine: has a unique real root \(\beta\in(1.8392,1.8393)\). This root is not a Pisot number

claims.text: Phase averages concentrate under the convolution but fade under Lebesgue measure.
claims.sourceLine: Their averages concentrate under the Bernoulli convolution while tending to zero in Lebesgue mean square.

claims.text: The criterion uses units with coefficients −1, 0 and 1.
claims.sourceLine: Their minimal polynomials have coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$, prescribed degree, and irreducible reduction modulo two.

claims.text: Singularity is equivalent to one-sided approximation at a fixed geometric rate.
claims.sourceLine: Singularity is equivalent to one-sided approximation by these retained targets at a fixed geometric rate.

claims.text: The criterion is an infinite approximation condition, not a finite algorithm.
claims.sourceLine: it is an infinite approximation condition, not a finite membership algorithm.
